bill.title: Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act of 2025

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects dairy producers and processors by expanding the types of milk schools may purchase and serve.
Schools participating in the lunch program face new training requirements and changes to meal planning and procurement rules.
Food service companies and suppliers to school meal programs would adjust product offerings to meet the expanded milk and nondairy beverage options.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would allow schools participating in the National School Lunch Program to offer whole milk and 2% milk to students, in addition to the low-fat and fat-free options currently required. It would expand nondairy milk alternatives, permit parents (not just doctors) to request milk substitutes for students with dietary restrictions, and exclude milk fat from saturated fat limits in school meals. The bill also requires annual food allergy training and certification for school food service staff.

plain.whoItTouches: Parents of young children. People who use food aid.

bill.title: Secure Rural Schools Reauthorization Act of 2025

industries.rationale: The program directly funds schools in rural counties containing federal land.
The program funds road construction and maintenance projects in affected counties.
Counties with federal land often have timber and mineral extraction activities that may be affected by resource advisory committee project decisions.

bill.plainSummary: This bill extends a federal program that sends payments to rural counties containing national forests and other federal land. The money helps fund local schools, roads, and municipal services. The bill provides payments through fiscal year 2026, including back payments for 2024 and 2025, and allows counties and advisory committees to continue initiating projects through 2028.

plain.whoItTouches: People who use public land, and people who live beside it.

bill.title: Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025
subjects: War crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity

industries.rationale: The bill creates new procedural pathways and limits defenses in civil litigation, expanding the scope and duration of claims that law firms may pursue or defend.
Museums and cultural institutions that hold or exhibit artwork are directly affected by expanded liability and procedural rules for restitution claims.
Banks and auction houses that handle art transactions or hold art as collateral face potential claims if works in their possession are subject to restitution.

bill.plainSummary: This bill removes the 2026 deadline for filing lawsuits to recover art and other property taken during Nazi persecution between 1933 and 1945. It makes it easier to sue foreign governments and defendants located anywhere in the United States, and it blocks certain legal defenses that courts have used to dismiss these claims, such as arguments that too much time has passed. The changes apply to cases already filed as well as future ones.

plain.whoItTouches: People who have been the victim of a crime.

bill.title: A joint resolution proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States relating to contributions and expenditures intended to affect elections.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: Organizations that spend money to influence elections would face new potential restrictions on their expenditures and fundraising.
The amendment would create new constitutional authority to regulate campaign finance, directly affecting election law practice and lobbying activity.
Limits on campaign spending could affect demand for political advertising across broadcast, digital, and print media platforms.
The amendment's authorization to distinguish between natural persons and corporations could affect how financial institutions participate in election-related spending.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment that would allow Congress and state governments to set limits on how much money candidates and others can raise and spend to influence elections. It would also permit lawmakers to treat corporations and other legal entities differently from individual people, including by prohibiting those entities from spending money on elections. The amendment would require ratification by three-fourths of the states to take effect.

bill.title: Stop Russian Market Manipulation Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

industries.rationale: The bill directly restricts imports of eight specific metals and minerals, affecting companies that source, process, or trade these materials.
Manufacturers that rely on platinum-group metals, nickel, copper, or zinc as inputs would face supply-chain changes and potentially higher costs.
Defense contractors use platinum-group metals and specialty alloys in aerospace and weapons systems, making supply sourcing relevant.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would ban the import of eight minerals—platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium, nickel, copper, zinc, and braggite—if they are produced in Russia or by Russian entities. The ban would also cover minerals obtained through swaps or other arrangements designed to evade the restriction. The prohibition would remain in effect until one year after the President certifies that Russia has ended hostilities against Ukraine, and would resume if Russia restarts hostilities within three years.

bill.latestActionText: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.
subjects: Drug safety, medical device, and laboratory regulation

industries.rationale: The bill directly targets insulin pricing and market practices, affecting pharmaceutical manufacturers' revenues and regulatory obligations.
Insulin cost caps or coverage mandates would alter health insurers' benefit design and reimbursement structures.
Changes to insulin pricing and access may affect prescribing practices and patient cost-sharing at the point of care.

bill.plainSummary: The bill's title suggests it addresses insulin pricing or access, likely building on previous INSULIN Act proposals that capped out-of-pocket costs for insulin users. Without the full text or detailed summary, the specific mechanisms—whether it imposes price caps, regulates manufacturer rebates, expands coverage mandates, or includes antitrust provisions—cannot be confirmed. The subject terms indicate it may involve competition rules, administrative enforcement, and oversight of drug pricing.
